case_name: State of Vindhya Pradesh (Now Madhya Pradesh) v Moradhwaj Singh and Others
petitioner: State of Vindhya Pradesh (Now Madhya Pradesh)
facts: The seventy-one appeals on certificates granted by the Judicial Commissioner of Vindhya Pradesh arise out of seventy petitions under art. 226 of the Constitution filed before that Court challenging the constitutionality of the Vindhya Pradesh Abolition of Jagirs and Land Reforms Act, No. XI of 1952.
Seventy (Nos. 40 to 109), out of these appeals, are by the State 'of Vindhya Pradesh (now Madhya Pradesh) while one (No. 110) is by the Brijindar Singh, a jagirdar.

The case of the petitioners in the Court of the Judicial Commissioner was that the Act was unconstitutional as various provisions in it placed an unreasonable restriction on the exercise of the fundamental rights guaranteed to the petitioners under Part III of the Constitution.
issues: Is the Vindhya Pradesh Abolition of Jagirs and Land Reforms Act, No. XI of 1952, constitutional?
Can a jagirdar be deprived of sir and khudkasht land without compensation?
Does s. 22(1) of the Act discriminate against jagirdars?
petitioner_arguments: The Act is unconstitutional as various provisions in it place an unreasonable restriction on the exercise of the fundamental rights guaranteed to the petitioners under Part III of the Constitution.
respondent_arguments: The Vindhya Pradesh legislature had full competence to make this provision under Entry 18, List II of the Seventh Schedule.
There is no question here of transgressing those powers and veiling the transgression under a pretence or disguise.
court_reasoning: The scheme of s. 22 is to give effect to s. 7(a) by which certain lands were allowed to remain in the possession of the jagirdar.
We have not been able to understand how these provisions can be called a piece of colourable legislation.
Applying this principle it is obvious that the Vindhya Pradesh legislature in this case had full competence to make this provision under Entry 18, List II of the Seventh Schedule.
holding: The seventy appeals by the State are dismissed; but as they were not pressed we think it right that the parties should bear their own costs of these appeals.
Appeal No. 110 is dismissed; but as it was not pressed we think it right that the parties should bear their own costs of this appeal.
